definition: Monastic means austerely simple and disciplined, like the life of monks.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word monastic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know monastic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The submarine crew kept a nearly monastic existence on patrol — narrow bunks, fixed watches, and months of enforced quiet.
A simple room just lacks clutter; monastic demands far more — bareness chosen on purpose and a rule to live by.
Spartan strips the comforts from the room; monastic goes further and strips them from the whole schedule, the meals, the company.
Cloistered outdoes even monastic: a monastic coder still walks to the office, while a cloistered nun never passes the convent wall.

An ascetic life gives up comforts on principle — plain food, hard beds, few possessions — usually in the name of spiritual or personal discipline. Monastic includes that self-denial but goes wider, naming a whole rule-governed way of living: fixed hours, silence, routine. Ascetic tells you what someone refuses; monastic tells you the regimen they follow.

Disciplined means governed by rules and self-control — a disciplined athlete trains on schedule whatever the weather. The word says nothing about plainness or withdrawal, and a disciplined life can be full of luxuries. Monastic requires both halves at once: the discipline and the bareness, appetites refused along with hours fixed.

Monastic says more than spartan: spartan describes only the bare furnishings, but monastic wraps the whole way of living — the fixed hours, the silence, the withdrawal from ordinary appetites — into one word.
A room can be spartan; a life is monastic.
Monastic borrows the monks' whole regimen — bare rooms, fixed hours, appetites refused — and needs no actual religion to work.
